intro: Chaliapin sings Rimsky-Korsakov’s Pushkin setting with Percy Pitt in an acoustic recording made in 1921. Compare the bass line’s pacing with his 1927 remake, without treating transfer brightness as vocal technique.
question: How does Chaliapin pace a dramatic song before the microphone?

cues.title: One bass, an orchestra
cues.text: Follow Chaliapin’s sustained vowels against the orchestral accompaniment. This is a bass solo with orchestra, not the original voice-and-piano setting; the balance reaching us also belongs to an acoustic recording and its later transfer.
cues.evidence: DAHR identifies bass with orchestra, Percy Pitt and the 10 October 1921 session: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/2000007905. The archive explicitly labels this transfer acoustic; no entrance is timed here.

cues.title: Words across the phrase
cues.text: In this opening stretch, compare the time Chaliapin gives to a sustained sound with the time taken by the next syllable. Phrase shape is a safer comparison with the remake than the amount of bass or treble in either transfer.
cues.evidence: The report places this in the opening span, with measured boundaries near 0:30 and 0:38. This is a listening question, not a claim about a particular Russian word or an isolated breath.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Pushkin, not an opera
cues.text: The label names Pushkin and Rimsky-Korsakov. The Prophet is the second of the composer’s Two Romances, Op. 49: Chaliapin’s dramatic delivery belongs here to a concert song rather than an operatic role.
cues.evidence: DAHR identifies the song and author; IMSLP lists The Prophet as Op. 49 No. 2: https://imslp.org/wiki/2_Romances,_Op.49_(Rimsky-Korsakov,_Nikolay).

cues.title: An early broad crest
cues.text: The recorded level rises through this stretch and remains comparatively high before dropping back. Listen across the whole rise rather than treating its strongest instant as the entire phrase.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/rimsky-korsakov-prophet-chaliapin-1921.txt: level rises from −17.0 dB at 1:15 to about −10 dB at 1:25–1:35, then falls to −17.5 dB at 1:40. These are relative levels within this transfer.

cues.title: Space before renewed pressure
cues.text: The quieter middle stretch gives the line a different scale. Compare the length of the withdrawal with the renewed intensity that follows; the 1927 remake need not spend the same amount of time between these points.
cues.evidence: The report measures a low-level span at 1:55–2:05, followed by a rise at 2:10. The comparison map follows the broad passage, not breaths or syllables.

cues.title: Another sustained rise
cues.text: Through this passage, the recorded level builds again. Keep the orchestral pulse in mind while following the bass line: a larger sound does not by itself tell us whether the tempo has changed.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −17.3 dB at 2:10 to approximately −10 to −12 dB at 2:30–2:40. Onset estimates do not establish the sung pulse.

cues.title: A brief withdrawal
cues.text: The sound recedes before rebuilding into the last large span. This quiet passage is also a less certain point in the automatic match with 1927; compare phrases, not a supposed exact syllable alignment.
cues.evidence: The report shows −25.6 dB at 2:50 before a rise towards 3:10. Alignment confidence falls below 0.8 at reference 174–175 seconds, corresponding to approximately 199–200 seconds in 1927.

cues.title: The final broad crest
cues.text: The last span sustains a high recorded level before the sound drops away. Follow how long the bass line carries its pressure, then distinguish the musical ending from the surface noise left on the transferred disc.
cues.evidence: The report lists 3:20–3:35 among the loudest five-second windows and a strong fall by 3:45. No precise final note, word or orchestral release is asserted.

facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.
composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
